Welcome back. Everything on this page runs real R in your browser — same setup as Coding Activities 1 and 2. You already know **ggplot2** from Activity 2; today you will **reshape tables** with dplyr and tidyr — filter rows, chain steps with pipes, and join metadata.

The first time you click **Run Code**, your browser downloads R once (a few seconds). After that it is quick.

## 1. Load the tidyverse

Coding Assignment 2 starts the same way. Run `library(tidyverse)` to load dplyr, tidyr, and friends. A conflicts message afterward is expected, not an error.

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: load_tidyverse
library()
```

::: {.hint exercise="load_tidyverse"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?library`: `library(package, ...)` attaches a package so its functions become available. Replace `package` with the name of the collection you need (dplyr, tidyr, and others ship together in one bundle).

Try `?library` in R for the full help page.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="load_tidyverse"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
library(tidyverse)
```

On DataHub and in your graded assignment you will type exactly this. The tidyverse also offers an older pipe, `%>%`; in this activity we use R's native pipe, `|>`.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: load_tidyverse
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("library\\s*\\(\\s*tidyverse\\s*\\)", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Load the tidyverse with `library(tidyverse)`."
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = "Tidyverse loaded. dplyr and tidyr are ready to use."
  )
}
```

## 2. Glimpse the penguins

`glimpse()` is a tidyverse way to inspect a dataset: rows, columns, and column types. Run it on `penguins` from the `palmerpenguins` package.

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| setup: true
#| exercise: glimpse_penguins
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: glimpse_penguins

```

::: {.hint exercise="glimpse_penguins"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?glimpse`: `glimpse(x)` — print a compact summary of a data frame (rows, columns, types).

Example with a built-in dataset:

```r
glimpse(mtcars)
```

Apply the same function to the dataset named in the exercise prompt.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="glimpse_penguins"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
glimpse(penguins)
```

You should see 344 rows and 8 columns. `species` and `island` are `<fct>` (categories); measurements like `body_mass_g` are `<dbl>` (numbers).
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: glimpse_penguins
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("glimpse\\s*\\(", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Call `glimpse(penguins)` to inspect the dataset."
  )
} else if (!grepl("penguins", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Pass `penguins` into `glimpse()`."
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = "344 rows, 8 columns — a tidy table ready to wrangle."
  )
}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check yourself

From the `glimpse()` output:

1. How many **rows** are there?
2. What **type** is `body_mass_g`?
3. Which column tells you **which island** each penguin was sampled on?

**Answers:** 344 rows; `body_mass_g` is `<dbl>`; `island`.
:::

## 3. Chain steps with a pipe

A **pipe** passes the result of one step into the next. R's native pipe is `|>`. Rewrite the nested version below as a pipe chain: start with `penguins`, keep only Adelie penguins with `filter()`, then `glimpse()` the result.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## `==` means "equals"

Inside `filter()`, **`==` checks whether two things match**. For example, `species == "Adelie"` keeps only rows where the species column is exactly `"Adelie"`.

Do not confuse `==` with a single `=`. A single `=` **assigns** a value to a name (`x <- 5` or `x = 5`). Double equals **`==` compares** — "is this equal to that?"
:::

Nested (hard to read):

```r
glimpse(filter(penguins, species == "Adelie"))
```

Your version should use `|>` twice.

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: first_pipe
penguins |>
  
```

::: {.hint exercise="first_pipe"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?filter`: keep rows where conditions are TRUE. Chain steps with `|>`:

```r
mtcars |>
  filter(cyl == 4) |>
  glimpse()
```

Use the same shape on `penguins`: start with the dataset, `filter()` to one group, then `glimpse()`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="first_pipe"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie") |>
  glimpse()
```

Read it top to bottom: "Take `penguins`, filter to Adelie, then glimpse." The pipe replaces nesting functions inside functions.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: first_pipe
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
has_pipe <- grepl("\\|>", code)
has_filter <- grepl("filter\\s*\\(", code)
has_glimpse <- grepl("glimpse\\s*\\(", code)
has_adelie <- grepl("Adelie", code)
if (has_pipe && has_filter && has_glimpse && has_adelie) {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = "Nice pipe chain. You filtered first, then inspected — same result, clearer code."
  )
} else if (!has_pipe) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Use the native pipe `|>` to connect at least two steps."
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Chain `penguins |> filter(species == \"Adelie\") |> glimpse()`."
  )
}
```

## 4. Filter out missing values

Two penguins have missing `body_mass_g`. Use `filter()` and `!is.na()` to drop those rows. Save the result as `penguins_clean`.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## `!` means "not"

The exclamation mark **`!` flips a yes/no test backwards**. The function `is.na(body_mass_g)` is `TRUE` when a value is missing. So **`!is.na(body_mass_g)`** means "body mass is **not** missing" — keep those rows.
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: filter_na
penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  
```

::: {.hint exercise="filter_na"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?filter`: `filter(.data, ...)` keeps matching rows. From `?is.na`: `is.na(x)` is `TRUE` for missing values; prefix with `!` to mean "not."

Example — drop rows with missing `mpg`:

```r
mtcars_clean <- mtcars |>
  filter(!is.na(mpg))
```

Use the same pattern on `penguins`, the column named in the prompt, and save as `penguins_clean`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="filter_na"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g))
```

You should have 342 rows — two fewer than the original 344.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: filter_na
#| check: true
if (!exists("penguins_clean", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "warning",
    message = "Save the filtered table as `penguins_clean`."
  )
} else {
  pc <- get("penguins_clean", envir = .envir_result)
  n <- nrow(pc)
  no_na <- sum(is.na(pc$body_mass_g)) == 0
  if (n == 342 && no_na) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = "342 rows, no missing body mass — ready for summaries and joins."
    )
  } else if (no_na && n < 344) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = paste0("Missing values removed (", n, " rows). Good to go.")
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Use `filter(!is.na(body_mass_g))` so rows with missing body mass are dropped."
    )
  }
}
```

## 5. Mean with a pipe

Compute the mean body mass of `penguins_clean`, skipping any remaining NAs with `na.rm = TRUE`. Use a pipe starting from `penguins_clean`.

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| setup: true
#| exercise: mean_pipe
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g))
```

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: mean_pipe
penguins_clean |>
  
```

::: {.hint exercise="mean_pipe"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?mean`: `mean(x, na.rm = FALSE)` — set `na.rm = TRUE` to skip missing values. From `?pull`: `pull(.data, var)` extracts one column.

Example pipe:

```r
mtcars |>
  pull(mpg) |>
  mean(na.rm = TRUE)
```

Start from `penguins_clean` and pipe to `mean()` on the body-mass column.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="mean_pipe"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
penguins_clean |>
  pull(body_mass_g) |>
  mean(na.rm = TRUE)
```

You should see about 4,002 g — the average weight across penguins with a recorded body mass.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: mean_pipe
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("mean\\s*\\(", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Finish the pipe with `mean(...)`."
  )
} else if (!grepl("na\\.rm\\s*=\\s*TRUE", code, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Include `na.rm = TRUE` inside `mean()`."
  )
} else if (is.numeric(.last_value) && length(.last_value) == 1 && !is.na(.last_value)) {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = paste0("Average body mass: ", round(.last_value, 1), " g.")
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Pipe from `penguins_clean` to `mean(..., na.rm = TRUE)` on body mass."
  )
}
```

## 6. Meet a wide table

On Coding Assignment 2 you will read a wide elevation table from a CSV file. Here we create the same kind of object directly — no file to read.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Wide island metadata (click to expand)

A **wide** table stores category names as **column headings**. Below is a tiny lookup table with fictional camp elevations (meters) for each study island:

```r
island_wide <- data.frame(
  Biscoe = 120,
  Dream = 85,
  Torgersen = 45
)
```

Notice: **Biscoe**, **Dream**, and **Torgersen** are column names, not values sitting in a row. That layout is easy to glance at in a spreadsheet but awkward for joining to `penguins` — we will reshape it in the next step.

On your graded assignment, the same wide layout arrives as a CSV; you will use `read.csv()` to load it. Today we build the object in memory so you can focus on reshaping and joining.
:::

Run this to create `island_wide`:

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: create_island_wide
island_wide <- data.frame(
  Biscoe = 120,
  Dream = 85,
  Torgersen = 45
)
island_wide
```

## 7. Reshape with `pivot_longer()`

Use `pivot_longer()` to turn the wide table into a **tidy** table: one row per island, with columns `island` and `camp_elevation_m`. Save as `island_tidy` and print it.

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| setup: true
#| exercise: pivot_longer
library(tidyverse)
island_wide <- data.frame(
  Biscoe = 120,
  Dream = 85,
  Torgersen = 45
)
```

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: pivot_longer
island_tidy <- island_wide |>
  
```

::: {.hint exercise="pivot_longer"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?pivot_longer`: `pivot_longer(data, cols, names_to, values_to, ...)`

Turn column names into values — example with a wide toy table:

```r
wide_mpg <- data.frame(
  four_cyl = 26.7,
  six_cyl = 20.1,
  eight_cyl = 15.1
)

wide_mpg |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "cyl_group",
    values_to = "avg_mpg"
  )
```

Apply the same arguments to `island_wide`, with the column names specified in the exercise.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="pivot_longer"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
island_tidy <- island_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "island",
    values_to = "camp_elevation_m"
  )
island_tidy
```

Three rows — one per island — with elevations in a column where R can match them to `penguins$island`.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: pivot_longer
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("pivot_longer\\s*\\(", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Use `pivot_longer()` to reshape the wide table."
  )
} else if (!exists("island_tidy", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "warning",
    message = "Save the result as `island_tidy`."
  )
} else {
  it <- get("island_tidy", envir = .envir_result)
  if (is.data.frame(it) && nrow(it) == 3 && "island" %in% names(it)) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = "Tidy island table — three rows, ready to join."
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Use `names_to = \"island\"` and `values_to = \"camp_elevation_m\"` with `cols = everything()`."
    )
  }
}
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Wide vs. tidy:** In Coding Assignment 2, population names sit in **column headings** of the elevation file — same problem, same fix with `pivot_longer()`.
:::

## 8. Join elevation onto penguins

Use `left_join()` to add `camp_elevation_m` to `penguins_clean`. Both tables share an `island` column — that is the key. Save the result as `penguins_joined`. Row count should stay 342.

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| setup: true
#| exercise: left_join
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g))
island_wide <- data.frame(
  Biscoe = 120,
  Dream = 85,
  Torgersen = 45
)
island_tidy <- island_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "island",
    values_to = "camp_elevation_m"
  )
```

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: left_join
penguins_joined <- penguins_clean |>
  
```

::: {.hint exercise="left_join"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?left_join`: `left_join(x, y, by = NULL, ...)` — add columns from `y` to `x` wherever a shared key matches.

Example:

```r
cyl_lookup <- data.frame(
  cyl = c(4, 6, 8),
  cyl_label = c("four", "six", "eight")
)

mtcars |>
  left_join(cyl_lookup, by = "cyl")
```

Join your cleaned penguin table to `island_tidy` on the column both tables share.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="left_join"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
penguins_joined <- penguins_clean |>
  left_join(island_tidy, by = "island")
nrow(penguins_joined)
```

342 rows, one new column — every penguin keeps its measurements and gains its island's camp elevation.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: wrangle_penguins
#| exercise: left_join
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("left_join\\s*\\(", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Use `left_join(island_tidy, by = \"island\")` in your pipe."
  )
} else if (!exists("penguins_joined", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "warning",
    message = "Save the joined table as `penguins_joined`."
  )
} else {
  pj <- get("penguins_joined", envir = .envir_result)
  if (is.data.frame(pj) && "camp_elevation_m" %in% names(pj) && nrow(pj) == 342) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = "Joined. 342 rows with a new `camp_elevation_m` column."
    )
  } else if (is.data.frame(pj) && "camp_elevation_m" %in% names(pj)) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = paste0("Join worked (", nrow(pj), " rows). Elevation column added.")
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Join `penguins_clean` with `island_tidy` using `by = \"island\"`."
    )
  }
}
```

## 9. Recap — verbs you practiced

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What does each function do?

| Function | Role |
|----------|------|
| `library(tidyverse)` | Loads dplyr, tidyr, and related packages |
| `glimpse()` | Quick look at rows, columns, and types |
| <code>|></code> | Passes data from one step to the next |
| `filter()` | Keeps rows that match a condition (with `==` or `!is.na()`) |
| `mean(..., na.rm = TRUE)` | Average of a numeric column, skipping missing values |
| `data.frame()` | Builds a wide table in memory — island names as column headings |
| `pivot_longer()` | Turns wide columns into tidy rows |
| `left_join()` | Adds columns from a second table by a shared key |

On **Coding Assignment 2** you will also use `read.csv()` to load the hemoglobin and elevation files from disk — same workflow, but the wide table arrives as a file instead of a `data.frame()` you type yourself.

If you can explain each row in your own words, you have covered the wrangling core of **Coding Assignment 2**.
:::

## 10. Transfer to Coding Assignment 2

On Canvas you will repeat this workflow with **hemoglobin** measurements and **population elevation** data:

1. `library(tidyverse)` and read `HumanHemoglobinElevation.csv`
2. `glimpse()`, `filter(!is.na(...))`, and `mean(..., na.rm = TRUE)`
3. Read `PopulationElevation.csv` (wide layout), `pivot_longer()`, then `left_join()`

Same functions, different biological story — altitude adaptation instead of penguin islands. You already practiced every wrangling step here.

The assignment also asks you to build a boxplot with `reorder()` so groups sort by elevation. You learned ggplot layering in **Coding Activity 2**; on Canvas you combine that with the joined table you prepare here.

No grading here. Try filtering to one species, chaining another summary through a pipe, or predicting how many rows a filter will leave before you run it.
